topic: Thread Unjoinability Requirement: Termination on Joinable Destruction
explanation: Assumption: RAII guarantees safe cleanup of asynchronous threads when a `std::thread` object goes out of scope. Reality: If a `std::thread` object is 'joinable' (meaning it is associated with a running thread of execution) when its destructor is called, the C++ standard dictates that the program must terminate via `std::terminate()`. This rule exists because the alternatives (implicit join or implicit detach) introduce worse, harder-to-debug problems related to performance or resource lifetime safety. Why It Fails: Failure to explicitly call `join()` or `detach()` before the `std::thread` object is destroyed results in immediate program termination, often happening when an exception causes early stack unwinding.
practical_example: A function launches a background thread, but an early exit condition (like an exception or a failed check) causes the function scope to close before `t.join()` is reached, leading to an unexpected crash.
chapter: Item 37: Remember that std::threads are not joinable upon destruction
book: Effective Modern C++ by Scott Meyers
